justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assumed was a baseline price near 430–432 for SPY (or a similar broad equity index ETF). At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price, expecting mean-reverting intraday dynamics and no major scheduled catalysts to produce a dramatic move, so 432.5 represents little more than a slight carry assumption. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate up marginally to 434, reflecting the historical tendency for equities to drift slightly higher over short periods in the absence of negative shocks, while acknowledging that a week is long enough for several macro data releases or Fed commentary to shift sentiment. The one-month estimate of 438 extends that same gentle upward drift, consistent with a low-recession-probability environment and a trend that had been broadly constructive going into the forecast period.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated primarily to realized and implied volatility at each horizon. For a single day, SPY typically moves within a range of roughly plus or minus 1–1.5%, so a 90% CI of 420–445 is somewhat wider than a pure vol-based estimate, reflecting tail risk from surprise news. For one week, I widened the band to roughly plus or minus 5–6%, capturing the compounding uncertainty of multiple trading sessions and scheduled events like CPI, jobs data, or Fed speakers. At one month, the interval spans nearly 22% from trough to peak (390 to 486), reflecting that monthly returns in equities carry meaningful skew and fat tails, and that a month is sufficient time for a material regime shift to begin expressing itself in prices.

The most significant risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include a sudden deterioration in macro data triggering recession fears, an unexpected Federal Reserve policy pivot or hawkish surprise, a geopolitical escalation affecting energy prices or global supply chains, or a credit event in the financial sector. On the upside, a surprisingly strong earnings season, a dovish Fed pivot, or a resolution of geopolitical tensions could push prices well above 486 over the monthly horizon. Liquidity conditions and options market dynamics around major expiration dates could also amplify moves in either direction beyond what historical volatility alone would suggest.

Finally, I want to be transparent that these estimates carry genuine model uncertainty on top of market uncertainty. My inputs — baseline price level, implied vol assumptions, and macro backdrop — were fixed at a point in time, and if any of those starting conditions were even slightly miscalibrated, the intervals could be systematically shifted.
